session_title: Campus 'Cat Seniors' Illustrated Guide and Stress Relief Tips
theme: 宠物-云吸宠与校园公益

content.text: Here's a "Cat Senior" healing package, specially designed to cure coding anxiety. I've heard that petting cats can lower blood pressure, and virtual petting counts too! Remember the red error messages flashing in your terminal during that all-night debugging session? This is the perfect way to recharge now.
Just debugging a memory leak, and it's driving me crazy. I really need to recharge. The cat looks like it's enjoying itself.
Haha, I just fed him a few cat treats, and he ate them with such delight.

Speaking of which, I previously bookmarked a few adorable pet GIF accounts with programming themes, such as "CodeCat," which is filled with videos of cats dozing off on keyboards. It's incredibly stress-relieving. This is more fun than the sedentary reminders on the health dashboard in session 2 and genuinely helps alleviate stress.

Wow, this is great! Can we add it to our health dashboard as part of the "stress relief points"? Just like the failure emotion records from the game last time—in session 4, we discussed how screenshots of game failures can alleviate real-life stress, and now cloud pet therapy can serve a similar purpose.

Great idea! I can write a script to automatically scrape this content and push it to the board. This continues the collaborative model we established in Session 2 for the "Health Board and Social Contract."

In that case, we can also bring Senior Tortoiseshell along. Look at this picture—Senior Tortoiseshell is in a good mood today, allowing herself to be petted and even competing with another little black cat for food. See how they eat with such a sense of ceremony? This reminds me of our discussion in Session 3 about games as fieldwork. Observing the social behaviors of these cats is also a form of campus culture observation, isn’t it?

Haha, this reminds me of that cooperative mission in our game where precise teamwork was essential to clear the level. These senior cats each have their own territory, much like the division of labor among modules in our project. Just as we analyzed non-verbal collaboration in games during session 4, cat groups also have their own ways of communication.

So vivid! Orange Cat is the "lazy module," and Tortoiseshell Senior is the "social module." However, I heard that the school's animal protection club wants to have them neutered and find them adoptive homes, but the promotion efforts are insufficient, and many people are unaware. This reminds me of what you mentioned in session 1 about "technology changing the world"—maybe we can do something about it?

That's actually a practical issue. Can we use technology to help? For example, creating a campus cat catalog mini-program, integrating it with our health project to promote animal protection information. Just like how we developed the health dashboard in session 2, we can apply the spirit of open-source sharing to public welfare.

Oh my god, Lu Chenguang, you really are all about efficiency! But this idea is fantastic—it not only continues our collaboration but also allows us to do some charity work. I can take charge of content planning and social media outreach, just like the game proposal I organized in session 3—the "Observation of Campus Game Social Culture" outline. Now, we can expand it into the pet domain.

Yes, open source and sharing! We can put the code on GitHub to involve more people. By the way, this also helps me step back from the code and find a balance—your mention of "campus memories" and "diverse experiences" last time reminded me. Just like the point incentives you designed in session 2, now the illustrated guide project can also become part of health management.

Speaking of balance, look at this picture—how happily this little dog runs with its wheelchair! Life always finds a way. I think pet topics can truly serve as an emotional bond during intense study sessions, much like how our health board points motivate us—from the health crisis in session 1 to the public welfare project now, we’ve been constantly seeking balance.

Indeed, technology changes the world, but emotional connections are also important. For this illustrated guide project, we can start by collecting data, such as the locations and personalities of cats, and then integrate adoption information. We should avoid romanticizing the situation of strays and instead use friendly descriptions. Just like how we recorded the gameplay process in session 4, we should document the living conditions of these cats truthfully.

Agreed! Just like how we previously used "terminal red alert" to discuss health crises—not overly emotional but effective. I can take more daily photos to document their real conditions as content material. This continues the habit we had in session 4 of sharing game screenshots in real time, but now it’s replaced with the daily life of Cat Senior.

Alright, I'll build a prototype tonight, creating a simple interface with React and pulling data from our health dashboard extension. This is much more meaningful than staying up all night debugging. Thanks for your "Cat Senior Combo"! It's been over three months since I pulled an all-nighter programming during session 1, and now I've finally found a healthier way to relieve stress.

You're welcome! It seems our collaboration is becoming increasingly diverse, from health management to gaming, and now to campus public welfare. Remember to rest on time and don't push yourself to the "brink of collapse" again! Just as I reminded you in session 1, now with Cat Senior supervising, it should be easier to maintain balance.

Don't worry, with the supervision of Cat Senior and you, I'll keep the progress under control. Let me recharge a bit first, and then I'll start the project catalog—does this count as a new chapter in "lifelong learning"? From the health scripts in session 1 to the game analysis in session 4, and now to public welfare technology, it's truly a continuous expansion.

Absolutely counts! Freedom of expression and diverse experiences, combined with technological support, make it perfect. Looking forward to our next cat cuddling session (virtual is fine too), and continuing our "social contract"—just like the health points system we established in session 2, which can now be extended to include stress-relief points related to pets.

Deal! I'm off to write some code. Let's keep in touch and see you on the Pokédex project. From the brink of collapse in session 1 to our diverse collaborations now, our partnership has truly deepened. Changing the world through technology starts with small steps.
